opus-5.5.text:
I think when Jensen says something like "generation 97," you shouldn't take the number too literally. He likes to make a point with a vivid image, and the point here is about iteration. A world model isn't something you build once and then you're done. It's more like a flywheel. You train a model, people use it to generate data, to evaluate policies, to train robots or autonomous vehicles. You learn where it breaks, where the physics looks wrong, where object permanence fails. You collect more data, curate it better, improve the tokenizer and the architecture, and train the next one. Every turn of that loop is a generation.

So my reading is that he's saying we're very early, but we're committed to running the loop many, many times. If you compare with large language models, the early GPT-style models were impressive demos, but it took many iterations, plus scaling of data, compute, and post-training, before they became broadly useful. World models are on a similar path, maybe even a harder one, because the physical world is much higher-dimensional than text. You have to get geometry, dynamics, contact, lighting, and causality roughly right, and you have to be consistent over long horizons.

There's also a second message. At NVIDIA we think of these as foundation models for physical AI, a platform others build on. If the platform improves every generation, then robotics companies, AV companies, and researchers can fine-tune for their own embodiment and their own tasks, and they all benefit from the progress. Number 97 just means: keep going, keep improving, and eventually the model becomes good enough that simulation with a learned world model is a real substitute for a lot of expensive, slow, sometimes dangerous real-world data collection.

Personally I find that framing motivating. As researchers we often want one breakthrough paper. But for something like a world model, the honest answer is that it's engineering plus research, compounded over many generations. If we do it right, someday we'll look back and the first versions will feel like the very early language models, important, but just the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says “generation 97” means they are committed to running the world-model improvement loop many times and to keep going and improving.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that Jensen is a very good storyteller, so when he says something like "generation 97," you shouldn't read it as a literal version number sitting in some internal document. I read it as a way of expressing how iterative this work really is. World models are not something you build once and ship. You train a version, you look at where it fails, you collect more data or you fix the architecture or you change the tokenizer or the training recipe, and then you train again. At NVIDIA we've been doing this for years now, since before the term "world model" became fashionable. When I look back at what we did with Cosmos and the generations before it, it genuinely feels like we've been through a huge number of iterations, and most of them were not announced. So the spirit of what he's saying is correct, even if the number is a little bit theatrical.

The second thing I'd take from it is a message about where the company is placing its bets. For a long time the industry was focused on language, because text is abundant and the loss function is clean. Physical AI is harder. The data is messier, the evaluation is harder, and you don't just need the model to be plausible, you need it to be physically consistent, so that a robot or an autonomous vehicle can actually act on its predictions. When Jensen talks about being many generations in, he's signaling that this is not a side project for us. We think the next wave of AI is about machines that understand the physical world, and the world model is the foundation layer for that, the same way the language model was the foundation layer for chatbots.

And the third thing, honestly, is that every generation taught us something that we didn't expect. Early on we thought scaling video generation alone would get us there. It helps, but it's not sufficient. You need the model to understand causality, to understand that if I push this object it moves and if I let go of it it falls. You need it to be controllable so that developers can condition on actions, on camera trajectories, on text. And you need it to be fast enough and open enough that people can actually use it in a simulation loop, not just make pretty videos. So if there is a generation 97, I'd say the lesson across all of those generations is humility. We keep finding that the physical world is richer than our models, and that's exactly why the work is interesting.

r001.rationale: The response describes world-model development as an ongoing cycle of training and iteration, says NVIDIA has worked on it for years, and calls it a major bet rather than a side project. This communicates persistence in developing world models.

astra-6.text:
My interpretation is that he’s emphasizing how early we are. I wouldn’t take “generation 97” as a literal roadmap with 97 clearly defined milestones. It’s a way of saying that world models will keep evolving through many iterations, and what we have today is only the beginning.

The deeper question is what improves from one generation to the next. Can a model go beyond producing something that looks plausible and actually predict how a world will respond to an action? Can it remain consistent over time and handle situations it hasn’t seen before? Those are the kinds of capabilities I would look for. So I hear that reference as a statement about the long trajectory ahead, rather than a specific arrival date.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models as having a long trajectory with many future iterations, but does not interpret the reference as expressing determination to persist in developing them.

sol-6.1.text:
My interpretation is that he’s emphasizing how early we are. I wouldn’t read “generation 97” as a precise technical milestone. It’s a way of saying that world models will evolve through many iterations, with each generation becoming better at understanding how the world changes and predicting what happens next.

The important distinction is between generating something that looks plausible and modeling something well enough that you can use it to make decisions. If an agent takes an action, can the model predict the consequences reliably? Can it handle situations it hasn’t seen before? Those are the capabilities I’d look at, rather than the generation number itself.

r001.rationale: The response frames “generation 97” as meaning world models will undergo many iterations, but does not convey determination or resolve to persist in developing them.
